summary: When discussing uncertainty estimates for the safe deployment of AI agents in the real world, the field typically distinguishes between aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. This dichotomy may seem intuitive and well-defined at first glance, but this blog post reviews examples, quantitative findings, and theoretical arguments that reveal that popular definitions of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties directly contradict each other and are intertwined in fine nuances. We peek beyond the epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty dichotomy and reveal a spectrum of uncertainties that help solve practical tasks especially in the age of large language models.

Bayes finally loses its place even in uncertainty quantification tasks 🥹
Quoting @fly51fly
[LG] Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know
S Kapoor, N Gruver, M Roberts, K Collins… [New York University] (2024)
- Large language models (LLMs) are often overconfident in their predictions, so we need good methods for estimating their uncertainties to know when to trust them.
- Some work argues prompting is sufficient for good uncertainties, while others introduce expensive sampling methods.
- This paper first shows prompting alone is insufficient, then demonstrates that fine-tuning on a small labeled dataset improves calibration and AUROC.
- Freezing an LLM's features for a linear probe is often insufficient, and training through the model (e.g. with LoRA) works much better.
- Good performance is possible with as few as 1000 labeled examples when training through the model.
- The resulting uncertainties generalize to new question types and even another model's generations, not just self-knowledge.
- A user study shows calibrated confidence scores affect whether people choose to agree with the LLM.

[1/3] 1/2 Here's my rough understanding of critical batch size
1. Increasing batch size can be seen as reducing the variance of the gradient estimator (via more compute).
2. With a smaller variance, you can use larger learning rate
3. With larger learning rate, you converge faster.
────────
[2/3] 2/2 However, the variance reduction will saturate at a certain critical batch size, and it's better to spend the compute running more iterations since the metric we care about is the number of gradient calls (rather than #iterations) to reach the target loss.
────────
[3/3] With that said, I think papers that study critical batch size should also consider swiping learning rate, and report loss v.s. FLOP / gradient evaluations under optimal learning rate for each batch size.

title: Xidulu (at COLM / SF this week) (@xidulu)
summary:
Why it sounds like rule based AI is coming back
Quoting @karpathy
We're missing (at least one) major paradigm for LLM learning. Not sure what to call it, possibly it has a name - system prompt learning?
Pretraining is for knowledge.
Finetuning (SL/RL) is for habitual behavior.
Both of these involve a change in parameters but a lot of human learning feels more like a change in system prompt. You encounter a problem, figure something out, then "remember" something in fairly explicit terms for the next time. E.g. "It seems when I encounter this and that kind of a problem, I should try this and that kind of an approach/solution". It feels more like taking notes for yourself, i.e. something like the "Memory" feature but not to store per-user random facts, but general/global problem solving knowledge and strategies. LLMs are quite literally like the guy in Memento, except we haven't given them their scratchpad yet. Note that this paradigm is also significantly more powerful and data efficient because a knowledge-guided "review" stage is a significantly higher dimensional feedback channel than a reward scaler.
I was prompted to jot down this shower of thoughts after reading through Claude's system prompt, which currently seems to be around 17,000 words, specifying not just basic behavior style/preferences (e.g. refuse various requests related to song lyrics) but also a large amount of general problem solving strategies, e.g.:
"If Claude is asked to count words, letters, and characters, it thinks step by step before answering the person. It explicitly counts the words, letters, or characters by assigning a number to each. It only answers the person once it has performed this explicit counting step."
This is to help Claude solve 'r' in strawberry etc. Imo this is not the kind of problem solving knowledge that should be baked into weights via Reinforcement Learning, or least not immediately/exclusively. And it certainly shouldn't come from human engineers writing system prompts by hand. It should come from System Prompt learning, which resembles RL in the setup, with the exception of the learning algorithm (edits vs gradient descent). A large section of the LLM system prompt could be written via system prompt learning, it would look a bit like the LLM writing a book for itself on how to solve problems. If this works it would be a new/powerful learning paradigm. With a lot of details left to figure out (how do the edits work? can/should you learn the edit system? how do you gradually move knowledge from the explicit system text to habitual weights, as humans seem to do? etc.).

MiMo-V2-Flash is live. It’s just step 2 on our AGI roadmap, but I wanted to dump some notes on the engineering choices that actually moved the needle.
Architecture: We settled on a Hybrid SWA. It’s simple, elegant, and in our internal benchmarks, it outperformed other Linear Attention variants on long context reasoning. Plus, a fixed KV cache just plays way nicer with current infra. Note: Window size 128 turned out to be the magic number (512 actually degraded performance). Also, sink values are non-negotiable—don't skip them.
MTP (Multi-Token Prediction): This is underrated for efficient RL. Aside from the first layer, it needs surprisingly little fine-tuning to hit high accept length. We didn't get to squeeze it into the RL loop this time due to deadlines, but it’s a perfect fit. We open-sourced the 3-layer MTPs so you can develop with it.
Posttrain with MOPD: We adopted On-Policy-Distillation from Thinking Machine to merge multiple RL models, and the efficiency gains were wild. We matched the teacher model's performance using less than 1/50th the compute of a standard SFT+RL pipeline. There’s a clear path here for a self-reinforcing loop where the student evolves into a stronger teacher.
Huge props to my team. They sculpted these ideas from scratch into production in just a few months.

[1/10] 1/ New work (with @hayou_soufiane and Eric) on Expert Specialization in MoEs:
We show that specialization arises from the similarity of hidden states, which is *complicated* e.g., optimizer dependent (adamw v.s. muon) and not always understandable 🙄
────────
[2/10] 2/ MoEs show "expert specialization", where text from different domains shows different expert activation patterns. We show that the similarity in expert usage is a consequence of hidden states geometry
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGCNu7SXsAAVgf0.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGCN7-_XQAAQi7D.jpg
────────
[3/10] 3/ Since the routers are just linear projections, we can actually prove the relationship. The inequality explains the **triangle** shape of the logit v.s. hidden states figure:
Similiar h --> Similiar Ph
Different h --> Similiar / Different Ph
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGC39b3X0AAdyov.png
────────
[4/10] 5/ For AdamW trained models, hidden states often become more correlated with depth, causing more concentrated and imbalanced expert usage. Fortunately, driven by load balancing loss, the router learns to suppress the "correlation direction": 1st right singular direction.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGC5trVWUAAkPMT.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGC7DUwboAAzB8c.jpg
────────
[5/10] 4/ So if your model is doing proper feature learning, and your router is not misaligned with your data, different tokens / sequences in different domains / context should have different hidden states, activating different experts.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGC9O-eaQAA5U_W.png
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGC9Qx9WkAAP4mz.png
────────
[6/10] 7/ We further prove how load balancing loss encourages the router to ignore the shared direction in the data
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGC_o2aW0AAUITz.png
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGC_sY3WkAAzuFE.png
────────
[7/10] 6/ Interestingly, for Muon trained models, e.g. Moonlight 16B / Trinity-Mini by @arcee_ai, we do not see such hidden states collapse. Also since these two models don't use auxiliary loss, their routers do not show suppression for the data's first singular direction
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGC75DcWAAAv3eF.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGC8R-lWoAAokyj.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGC8UBJXcAARKqx.jpg

We provide a couple of counterintuitive examples, e.g., duplicating inputs can make different inputs use similiar experts:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGDAHwbWAAAouGW.jpg
────────
[9/10] 10/ In summary, expert specialization is important to have, as it tells you: (a) You are doing proper feature learning; (b) Your router is data aware. However, the hidden states space / expert specialization may not necessarily have interpretable features we can utilize.
────────
[10/10] 9/ Or... on gpt-oss (with chat template), text on different topics activates **same** expert during pre-filling, but the usage starts to diverge when rollout begins

- Setting threshold values for uncertainty signals is hard.

────────
[2/7] 3/ Solution: we use a validation set, and we ask the user to specify an *interpretable* target risk they can tolerate (e.g. 10% of incorrect exit). Then our algorithm searches over all (threshold, signal) pairs to find the **most efficient** criteria that meets the goal

It's hard because the uncertainty metrics are neither calibrated nor interpretable.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIYT7meWcAAyLfm.jpg

[4/7] 5/ The lower threshold is parameterized by a sigmoid shape function, with parameters learned on the validation set, given a user-specified "false negative risk": How many incorrect deferral the user wants to afford

Stop if no progress.
Instances stopped this way will later be deferred to human experts, as they may be unsolvable by the LLM.

summary:
Stochastic optimization 101:
Larger batch size / control variate accelerate convergence by **enabling larger step sizes**
Quoting @gurtej__gill_
I spent my morning reading this new paper on batch scaling in LLM Reinforcement Learning.
And i feel it addresses the bad habit of cranking up batch sizes just because our GPUs look underutilized.
The authors simply just separate the systems side from the algorithmic side.
We all know autoregressive rollout generation is heavily memory-bandwidth-bound at low concurrency, so jumping to a larger batch gives you an immediate, satisfying throughput jump (they hit up to 2.29× on fixed hardware).
But because each step now burns far more samples, you easily end up trading away learning efficiency.
Their rule of thumb is that a bigger batch only cuts down real wall-clock time if your throughput gains actually outrun that sample penalty.
The most practical takeaway for anyone running GRPO or PPO is their square root learning rate scaling under Adam.
Across a bounded window (B to 4B), retuning the learning rate kept sample efficiency steady and slashed time-to-target by 29%.
If you leave the learning rate alone, the higher throughput is an illusion and you actually train slower.

clean_summary:
Looped language models (LMs) usually require more parameters and memory as they loop through computations. Xidulu suggests these models could use three times fewer parameters and a three times smaller key-value cache while still matching standard Transformer performance.

The idea centers on the fixed point of the loop, a stable state the model reaches. By introducing fixed-point shortcuts, looped LMs can add more computation (FLOPs) without increasing memory. Two techniques—learned depth prior and orthogonal injection—help shape these fixed points during training and inference, making looped LMs more efficient in both pre-training and decoding.
